links.note: Greek says “Nicodemus was his name”; English uses “named Nicodemus.”
English names Jesus where Greek refers to him with a pronoun.
English adds a copula to describe the one who has come as a teacher.
English compresses “answered and said” into “answered.”
English expands the participle “being” into “when he is.”
“All” makes the Greek plural “you” explicit.
English compresses “answered and said” into “answered.”
English compresses “answered and said” into “answered.”
Greek puts γὰρ second; English puts “For” first.
“He” is inside the verb: the ending of ἔδωκεν means “he gave.”
Greek has “the Son”; “his” is the translator’s reading of the article.
Greek says “everyone who believes.”
“Should” carries the verb’s subjunctive mood.
English uses a possessive where Greek has the article “the.”
Greek coordinates Jesus and his disciples; English uses “with.”
English compresses “answered and said” into “answered.”
Greek expresses “nothing” through concordant negatives: “not ... not even one.”
The cognate phrase “rejoices with joy” intensifies the rejoicing.
English repeats the necessity understood in the second clause.
Greek says “is from”; English expresses origin as belonging.
“Set his seal to this” renders the single Greek verb “sealed.”
English names God as the subject of the otherwise unnamed giver.
